newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia raises sell-off plans, parliament protests.
newsitem.headline: Russia raises sell-off plans, parliament protests.

text.p: Russian privatisation may take a leap ahead next week if terms are set for its biggest sale yet, but critics in the Communist-dominated parliament said on Thursday the sell-off had been riddled with errors.

Privatisation minister Alfred Kokh told the Duma lower house of parliament that an auction open to foreigners for 25 percent of Svyazinvest, the monster telecommunications holding company that controls most regional telecom firms, may be announced next Tuesday.
Russia, suffering from a budget crunch which is forcing 30 percent cuts in budget spending, expects to raise well over $1 billion by selling the stake.
It has also removed a number of oil companies from a list of strategic firms which may not be privatised and will sell stakes of them at auctions open to foreigners, Kokh said.
"Foreign capital will come into the country come what may," he told a news conference, warning that foreigners would make shady deals to get to Russia if they were not given free entry.
The Duma for its part condemned the entire privatisation process, which was begun in 1992 by current reform chief and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly.
"The country suffered considerable losses from the privatisation of state and municipal property at give-away prices," said a Duma bill, passed in a first reading.
The bill, which is not binding on the government, said privatisation had often broken the law.
The Duma said the courts should rule on privatisations that brought billions of dollars in budget revenues, but were widely criticised for insider trading and lack of transparency.
A previous attempt to sell a Svyazinvest stake fell through in late 1995.
Russia is still scraping to find new sources of revenue that will not hurt prospects for economic growth. No growth is now expected this year, but hopes are higher for 1998.

A government budget plan for 1998 looks to the West for funding in the form of credits, such as $3 billion in Eurobonds which Russia expects foreign investors to snap up, though it hopes to be able to borrow domestically at low rates, too.
The privatisation ministry has been told to bring in more money in 1997 and Kokh said he planned to roughly double forecast privatisation revenues to raise about 11.5 trillion roubles this year.

He said plans were almost ready to sell part of Rosneft, the final major oil company still completely in state hands, and said he had discussed privatisation of Aeroflot national airlines and the VDNKh exhibition park, socialism's showcase in the Soviet Union but now a popular trade centre.
But he did not dismiss the Duma's criticism out of hand.
"There are a number of interesting proposals, and if those remain in the next draft, I don't think it would be worse off," he said.

But the government appears ready to forge ahead with privatisation, just as it appears ready to cut budget spending without the approval of the Duma, which is considering budget cuts that are already being made.
"To change the course of privatisation is only possible with the agreement of the executive branch," Kokh said.
